content.text: Recently, many organizations have released machine learning models trained on massive datasets (GPT-3, YOLO, etc...). This is a great contribution to science and streamlines modern AI research. However, publicizing these models allows for the potential "reverse engineering" of models to uncover the training data for the model. Specifically, an attacker can download a model, look at the parameter values and then try to reconstruct the original training data. This is particularly bad for models trained on sensitive data like health information. In this section we are going to use randomness as a method to defend against algorithmic "reverse engineering."
